name: Buddha Jayanti in Lumbini
image_query: Buddha Jayanti Lumbini Maya Devi celebration
when: Full moon of Baisakh, late Apr–May
summary: Buddha Jayanti, the full moon of the Nepali month of Baisakh, marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death. In Lumbini, his birthplace, it brings processions, chanting by monks from many countries, butter lamps around the Maya Devi Temple and tens of thousands of pilgrims.
body: Buddha Jayanti, also called Buddha Purnima, falls on the full moon of Baisakh, which lands between late April and late May. Theravada tradition holds that the Buddha's birth, his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and his passing at Kushinagar all happened on this full moon. Lumbini, as the birthplace, holds Nepal's largest celebration, with national leaders, foreign delegations and pilgrims from India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Tibet and beyond arriving in the days before.

The day begins early in the Sacred Garden, where monks and nuns from the monastic zone gather for chanting near the Maya Devi Temple and the bodhi tree. Processions carry Buddha images along the central canal and between monasteries, and many temples hold special pujas, dharma talks and free meals. In the evening, butter lamps and candles are lit around the Puskarini pond and in monastery courtyards. Nepali Buddhists, especially Newar and Tamang communities, travel from across the country.

The festival falls in the hottest season, with afternoon temperatures often near 40 °C, so the most rewarding hours are dawn and dusk. Hotels in Lumbini and Bhairahawa fill well ahead, and security is tight around the Sacred Garden when dignitaries attend. Many pilgrims combine the day with a quieter visit to Tilaurakot or Ramagrama before or after.
tips: Book Lumbini hotels two to three months ahead, as rooms sell out for the days around the full moon.
Reach the Sacred Garden before 6 am for chanting, before the heat and the largest crowds arrive.
Carry water, a hat and light white or pale clothing; afternoon temperatures can approach 40 °C.
Expect security checks and some closures when national leaders or foreign delegations attend the main ceremony.

faqs.q: When is Buddha Jayanti in Lumbini?
faqs.a: Buddha Jayanti falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Baisakh, usually between late April and late May. The date changes every year with the lunar calendar. It is a public holiday in Nepal, and celebrations in Lumbini begin the day before. Check current status before you travel to confirm the year's date.

faqs.q: What happens at Lumbini on Buddha Jayanti?
faqs.a: Monks and nuns gather for chanting at the Maya Devi Temple, processions carry Buddha images through the monastic zone, monasteries hold special prayers and free meals, and butter lamps are lit around the sacred pond at dusk. National leaders often attend a formal ceremony, and pilgrims arrive from across Asia.

faqs.q: Is it a good idea to visit Lumbini on Buddha Jayanti?
faqs.a: For pilgrims, yes; it is the most meaningful day of the year to be at the birthplace. Expect crowds, heat near 40 °C, security checks and higher hotel demand. If you prefer quiet reflection, visit a few days before or after, when monasteries are still decorated but crowds are smaller.

faqs.q: Is Buddha Purnima the same as Buddha Jayanti?
faqs.a: Yes. Buddha Jayanti and Buddha Purnima are two names for the same full moon festival, also known internationally as Vesak. In India it is usually called Buddha Purnima; in Nepal both names are used. Some countries, such as those following the Chinese calendar, mark the Buddha's birthday on a different date.

name: Bhagwati Jatra in Tansen
when: Day after Krishna Janmashtami, Aug–early Sep
summary: Palpa's biggest festival pulls the chariot of the goddess Bhagwati through Tansen's steep lanes on the day after Krishna Janmashtami, in memory of the 1815 victory over British forces during the Anglo-Nepal war. It has been held for over two centuries and draws crowds from across the district.
body: The Rana Ujeshwori Bhagwati Temple in Tansen was built in 1815 by Colonel Ujir Singh Thapa after his troops defeated East India Company forces at Jit Gadhi near Butwal during the Anglo-Nepal war. Ever since, the town has celebrated the victory with a festival for the goddess, held on the day after Krishna Janmashtami, which falls in August or early September. Local reports describe it as the largest jatra in Palpa, and the provincial government declares a district holiday for it.

On the day, the goddess is carried in a decorated wooden chariot through the old town, hauled on ropes by devotees from the temple through the main lanes and squares. Traditional musicians, local officials and crowds of families accompany it, and houses along the route hang out flags and offerings. The steep, narrow streets make the procession slow and dramatic, with sudden surges as the chariot is pushed uphill.

Because the festival falls in the monsoon, the day can be wet and the views from Srinagar hill are usually hidden. The trade-off is seeing Tansen at its most crowded and devout, with few foreign visitors present. The festival also connects to Butwal's Jit Gadhi fort and to the wider story of the Anglo-Nepal war that shaped Nepal's southern border.
tips: Book Tansen rooms well ahead; Hotel Srinagar and old-town guesthouses fill with Nepali visitors.
Watch from a raised doorway or balcony, as crowds press hard around the chariot on steep lanes.
Carry an umbrella and wear shoes with grip, since monsoon showers make the stone streets slippery.
Check the Siddhartha Highway for landslides before driving up from Butwal or down from Pokhara.

faqs.q: When is the Bhagwati Jatra in Tansen?
faqs.a: The Bhagwati Jatra is held on the day after Krishna Janmashtami, which follows the lunar calendar and usually falls in August or early September. The provincial government declares a public holiday in Palpa district for it. Dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What does the Bhagwati Jatra celebrate?
faqs.a: It honours the goddess Bhagwati and commemorates Nepal's 1815 victory over East India Company forces at Jit Gadhi near Butwal during the Anglo-Nepal war. Colonel Ujir Singh Thapa built the Bhagwati Temple in Tansen in thanks, and the chariot procession has been held for more than 200 years.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Bhagwati Jatra?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch the chariot procession and visit the temple, and local people are usually happy to explain the rituals. Dress modestly, keep a respectful distance from the chariot ropes unless invited to pull, and ask before photographing people at worship.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Tansen?
faqs.a: August is monsoon season, so expect rain, cloud and hidden mountain views, and possible landslides on the roads. If you want to see the Bhagwati Jatra, it is worth it. For mountain views and dry walking, visit from October to March instead.
